Review Body: The Body Keeps the Score: Brain, Mind, and Body in the Healing of Trauma by Bessel Van Der Kolk, M.D. felt like being in therapy and studying the therapy technique at the same time. At about the 20% mark, I think, I texted a psychologist friend and arranged a book discussion for when I finished it. The research Van De Kolk has participated in over his career is fascinating as is the other research he gathered in this book. I repeatedly wished I'd found this research twenty or thirty years ago. That said, there were several times word choices that made me feel uncomfortable and earlier in my life likely would have been triggering for me. I'm certain the research has continued to evolve as research tends to do, but The Body Keeps the Score made me finally realize that all those times I felt like my body was betraying me was it having a normal reaction to trauma. Several of the life techniques discussed in the book, I discovered through a more painstaking and lonely process of trial and error and for different reasons. The Body Keeps the Score is a reminder that nothing happens in a vacuum and that trauma inflicted today will resurface someday, especially if it goes unrecognized and untreated. Overall, I found the research compelling but also noticed there seems to be a glaring hole in the research related to the trauma victims who lived through the wars that affected the soldiers the research concentrated on so much. I would highly recommend The Body Keeps the Score for anyone interested in the research behind how trauma is stored in the body and why the body reacts the way it does to trauma.

Review Date: Reviewed in the United States on December 13, 2023
Review Body:
The Body Keeps the Score: Brain, Mind, and Body in the Healing of Trauma by Bessel van der Kolk, MD, is a seminal work in the field of trauma and its treatment. This book is not just a scientific exploration of how trauma affects the brain and body, but also a compassionate guide to the paths of recovery. Dr. Van der Kolk, with decades of experience in the field, integrates his research findings with real-world case studies, offering a comprehensive view of trauma’s impact.

One of the book's most significant contributions is its emphasis on how trauma physically alters the brain and body. Dr. Van der Kolk eloquently explains complex neurological and psychological concepts, making them accessible to both professionals and lay readers. He challenges traditional approaches to treating trauma, arguing for more holistic and body-centered therapies. This perspective is refreshing and eye-opening, underscoring the limitations of relying solely on talk therapy and medication.

The book delves into various innovative treatment methods, such as Eye Movement Desensitization and Reprocessing (EMDR), yoga, and neurofeedback, highlighting the importance of integrating body and mind in the healing process. These insights are invaluable for therapists, patients, and anyone interested in understanding and managing the effects of trauma.

However, some readers might find the book's detailed descriptions of traumatic experiences difficult to read. Additionally, while Dr. Van der Kolk critiques certain established treatment methods, he does so respectfully, contributing constructively to the ongoing conversation about mental health care.

In summary, The Body Keeps the Score is a groundbreaking and empathetic work that offers hope and guidance for those affected by trauma. It’s a must-read for anyone interested in psychology, mental health, and the transformative power of healing trauma. Dr. Van der Kolk's compassionate approach and extensive knowledge make this book a valuable resource and a beacon of hope for many.

Review Date: Reviewed in the United States on July 13, 2023
Review Body:
Wow! The Body Keeps the Score has so much information in it! I’m not great at reading technical books, especially if they are science related. Yeah. I’m more of a language arts and social studies kind of gal! I have gotten better since I taught sixth grade science, but technical brain stuff still confuses me a bit. Thankfully, Bessel Van Der Kolk does his best to explain things so that even I can understand them. I may have needed to reread some paragraphs a couple of times, but I did finally understand it.

The Body Keeps the Score is so well written. Like I said, even I was able to understand it. The writing style may be more technical, but it is still usually easy to understand. If you’re like me and know very little about the brain, you’ll be good! He does a good job of explaining all the different parts of the brain and how trauma affects each of those parts.

I learned a lot from the examples he shares of his clients and how they have reacted to traumatic experiences. It’s crazy how the same situation can cause such different reactions! In one person the experience can cause the person’s brain to pretty much shut down, while someone else’s brain in the same experience can cause more of a fight or flight response. I did find it fascinating to learn about these different responses.

One of the reasons I’m glad I read The Body Keeps the Score is so that I will be better prepared and be better able to help my friends, family members, and students who have suffered from traumatic experiences. One of my favorite parts was learning about all the different strategies that can be used to help people heal from their trauma. I knew about a few of them, but I learned about several unconventional methods that will help.

I love that healing focuses on body awareness and mindfulness. It’s all about separating the past and the present and becoming aware of your body. It seems strange, but apparently when you suffer from a traumatic experience, your past and present collide. When something triggers your mind in the present, you feel the same emotions as you did when you first had the experience. At that point it becomes difficult to discern if you are in the present or in the past. Fascinating, right?

Content Rating: PG
-Profanity: None
-Intimacy: Low (Incest and abuse are noted as causing trauma.)
-Violence: Low (He does describe some traumatic experiences his clients have experienced.)
Age Recommendation: 16+ (It’s quite technical and younger readers may not fully understand the content or be able to apply the knowledge. There are heavier themes that may not be appropriate for younger readers.)

Review Date: Reviewed in the United States on December 10, 2022
Review Body:
Trauma, says van der Kolk results from a person being put in an emotional, dangerous situation from which they can't escape: a war, child sexual abuse, partner abuse, etc. This changes their brain and can cause all sorts of problems. People get diagnosed with Attention Deficit Disorder, Oppositional Disorder, Dissociative Disorder, etc. Often, those are treated with drugs. But that usually only gets at the symptoms of what's really wrong. Talk therapy also generally fails. He quotes (I paraphrase) one patient, "I already know I make bad decisions and do things that hurt me. Cognitive therapy makes me think I'm broken and unlovable."

So what works? One must in some way re-experience the trauma--the emotions, the way it felt physically--but in a safe, accepting environment. "Being validated by feeling heard and seen is a precondition for feeling safe." (p. 303) He devotes several chapters to therapies that he says cure: Eye Movement Desensitization and Processing (EMDR), yoga, Internal Family Systems (IFS), PBSP psychomotor therapy, biofeedback, drama therapy.

It is an impressive work that has become a classic. Van der Kolk writes well, and the many stories of successful patients make it almost impossible to lose interest. But ... but ... it just seems too neat. The therapies he likes always seem to work. They don't just make things better; they actually cure. He comes across as superman, always successful, always curious, always able to accept what works and reject what doesn't, no matter what anyone else says. There are hundreds, maybe thousands of references in the back. backing up what he writes. But many of them date to the replication crisis, when the academic need to publish, publish, publish led to many articles reporting results that could not be replicated.

The copyright says 2014, which means it was probably written in 2013 with most of the research from earlier. I would love to see a second edition or a volume of critical (but fair) essays.

Review Body: Excellent book for understanding how truly controversial the field of psychiatry is around trauma diagnoses and treatments. I can personally attest to the authenticity of the author’s portrayal of clinician reluctance or squeamishness in diagnosing and treating trauma or even just recognizing trauma symptoms or a particular organization of symptoms as valid in their own right, worthy of viable labeling and inclusion in the future versions of the DSM for psychiatry. Misdiagnosis is a real and traumatic experience for people who survive traumatic events and enter into psychiatric care for answers, and furthermore, is something we need to push against as consumers of mental health care. Vanderkolk is very intelligent and compassionate. I think most readers will understand and appreciate what he is trying to convey to survivors and professionals alike with respect to the far-reaching nature of enduring traumatic experiences and the ethical implications of treating trauma in clinical practice, among other things. The author has included highly personal stories for readers to gather a sense of what is happening in real time with this mental health issue. Readers begin to understand that the human brain retains traumatic experience indefinitely and this can and does present a vast social dilemma, one worthy of honest inclusion in viable treatments and funding for research. My only complaint or discomfort with the book is that at times I sense the author’s approach in revealing clinical data gets bogged down by, or clouds the narrative. Feels like reading a medical paper or an article from a journal, leaving something to be desired. After reading The Body Keeps the Score, you will definitely view psychiatry in a different light, either positive or negative depending upon your individual experiences, and you will view the human brain/body connection in a different light. An insightful and deeply meaningful book.

Review Body:
”Change begins when we learn to ‘own’ our emotional brains. That means learning to observe and tolerate the heartbreaking and gut-wrenching sensations that register misery and humiliation.”

“The Body Keeps the Score” is a comprehensive study of emotional trauma: its physiology, psychological effects, social ramifications, historical contexts, and most promising treatments. Dr. Van der Kolk speaks with authority and compassion earned through five decades of pioneering research and patient care, illustrating most of his points with personal anecdotes that breathe life into the pages. For those who suffer from traumatic wounds, he offers validation and hope. Their care team he empowers with an astonishing wealth of research, culminating in holistic, evidence-based treatment options: art, writing, music, dance, yoga, Emotional Freedom Technique (EFT), Eye Movement Desensitization and Reprocessing (EMDR), Internal Family Systems therapy (IFS), neurofeedback, and acting.

”Imagination gives us the opportunity to envision new possibilities—it is an essential launchpad for making our hopes come true. It fires our creativity, relieves our boredom, alleviates our pain, enhances our pleasure, and enriches our most intimate relationships… Without imagination there is no hope, no chance to envision a better future, no place to go, no goal to reach.”

Van der Kolk’s research legitimizes holistic treatments, and his concrete examples drawn from real therapy sessions bring those methods to life. He instills hope that one of many of these techniques will bring trauma sufferers back to life, too.

What you will not find here is any mention of spirituality. It’s understandable that the author would steer clear of the topic, given his focus on academic research and his professional audience, but I found that its lack leaves a vast hole in his message. He provides tools for alleviating irrational suffering, but hope stops there: with the too-often disappointing materialistic “reality” that we all face. Persistent meaning lies beyond our emotions, beyond our intellect, in the realm of faith, unity, or emptiness. From these transcendent foundations, the horror of trauma wanes, our perspective broadens, and we draw the strength to heal ourselves.

This is a must-read for those who treat victims of trauma, but it neglects the spirit and should be supplemented with a transcendent path.

Review Body: Once again, I rarely ride the wave of book popularity often arriving to read a book in its waning years. Nonetheless, I am quite happy to offer my opinion on the “Body Keeps the Score”. My first reaction is that the book is much longer than it needs to be—particularly the hundreds of pages dedicated to describing and historically detailing traumatic stress from every imaginable angle and then some. Despite this caveat, I found the author’s arguments compelling and his concern for the suffering of so many trauma sufferers genuine—I found his many real-life stories deeply moving. Having been subjected to trauma in first person and having worked personally and professionally with others who suffer PTSD, I do recognize with the author that the current diagnostic framework is inadequate. While medicine may not be the best solution, it is most certainly not a cure all for victims. Unfortunately, pharmacology’s profit margins seem to outweigh many patients’ actual needs. As a Christian I am well aware of the soul, mind, body connection and know the power of working with a person at every level to foster spiritual, mental, and physical harmony. I appreciated learning about the new and ‘traditional’ therapeutic and wholistic approaches that the author shares from his vast experience of working with trauma victims. I pray that this book may reach those for whom it is intended and that it will serve as a catalyst for much needed healing in our all too broken world.

Review Body: I finally finished "The Body Keeps the Score" after a months-long relationship with it. It's very interesting, but also lengthy, and quite clinical/educational-leaning. I learned that a summary book, as well as a workbook, are also available. So if the topic of how your past shows up in your present, give it a read. I hesitate to use the word 'trauma' because it's so over-used and has the stigma of abuse associated with it. But trauma is not always physical; it is mental and emotional too. Even a childhood in which you were ignored and forced to take care of your own needs is still considered trauma. And this shapes not only behavior, but thoughts and emotions that stay with you forever.

It is wildly triggering and this is why I say one should be actively going to therapy to work through the heaviness of this book if they truly want to let go of all the things holding them back in life, as described in the book trauma can leave you frozen in time. Review Body:
This is a good book—I feel like it’s dead on when it comes to its criticism of masking the effects of childhood trauma with a buffet of disorders. However, it ends on such a strange note for a book that details horrible sexual assaults on children, with an anecdote about a man being able to orgasm with a partner after a certain therapy. Throughout the book, I felt like the focus on sexual assault was to balance the minimization of it in the context of PTSD that has been so prevalent in, well, all cultures. But… it was just so off putting to me that the final proof of the hope for healing trauma was the achievement of an orgasm. It made me question some of the rest.

Overall, that’s a minor criticism and I think this is an important book that many should read, especially if they work in any capacity with “problem” (abused/traumatized?) children or young adults.
